chapter: Emmett Hardy, Bix and the Rhythm Kings
title: Hardy's last playing, the gift of his horn and his funeral
summary: At Hardy's birthday he plays the blues with his mother, gives Hazel his cornet, and dies soon after; a huge funeral crosses by ferry.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: He didn't touch the horn. He gave me the horn. That's how I come and start playing the corner. When he, when he, when he, he gave me, yeah, well we, uh, it was his, uh, it was his, uh, 21st birthday. And in, in the meantime, uh, uh, the Eckert band had, had split up. Uh, half of the band went with Tony Forgerat. And, uh, and the other half of the band I had, uh, the original piano player and a kid by the name of Elroy Mazur on saxophone. And I went to Leon Primer's house and got Leon with it, was 16 at the time. And he knew two tunes. Yes, we have no bananas and the jasmine blues. That was his, that was his repertoire. And, uh, I went to Leon's house and got Leon. And we taught him all the tunes. So we go up to Emmert's house for this birthday party. Now the Boswell girls were there. And, uh, and, uh, Leon Primer, Bill Eckert, Elroy Mazur, a couple of guys myself. So we were playing and, uh, finally he goes, he can, I got to see him arguing with his mother, you see. Cause the doctors had forbid him to touch the horn, you see. And so finally he goes in the closet and he gets, comes out with this square case, the, what's your call them, Victor model cornet, you see. Yeah, you know the old Victor model. So he, uh, he takes it out and his mama sits at the piano. And they start playing, his mama starts hitting those church chords, you know. And they start playing the blues. Well Bill, you never, you never heard such blues in all your life. And they wound up with, us sitting around the floor crying like babies. The guy, he played so beautiful. He played so beautiful. He played so beautiful. If, if, this Emmert and his mother, that's all. If there's such a thing as a guy knowing that was going to be the last time he was in ever play and he, and put it in there, he did. And I saw that, I saw that same thing happen again to another guy in New York later on. A guy, uh, by the name of Slats Hope, a trombone player, that, uh, committed suicide. And we had a session, just about three hours before he committed suicide. And the same thing, he played better than he ever played. And this guy used to play like Dawson Pretty, you know. And played just as pretty as Jimmy, as Tommy ever played. Uh, in fact, he used to play more like, like, Troop. I don't know whether you ever heard Troop. George Troop, Trombone, oh, beautiful, beautiful trombone. He come out of that Henry Thies band. You remember that WW, uh, WLW in Cincinnati was the staff band? Oh yeah, I've heard of that. For years and years, Henry Thies. Well this guy, this, this trombone player, come out of that band. Well anyway, they play, oh they must have played for an hour. Just the blues. And when he got through, he took the horn, he put it in the box, and he closed the box, and he handed it to me, he said, here Mark, I won't have no more use for this. So that was, that's how I come to get the horn. You still got that? No, it got, no it got burned up in the, in the, in the silver slip of fire. I got one just like it. But that, that, that original horn, it got burned up in the silver slip of fire. Uh, the first, that got burned out down there three times. But that, that, that was the first one. And, uh, and then I think it was a week or two weeks after that, after this birthday party, that he died. It was very, I know, it was not, not longer than, than, than, in two weeks. Well, that's the longest funeral I ever saw in my life, Bill. They buried him in Gretna. And they lived right back State Street here. You know where Willow Street is, Dick? Yeah, I'm sure. Well, they lived right on, you know, that's where, where the, where the street comes by that, the convent. You know, that, the Ursuline Convent, I think it is. The street comes, and when it gets to State Street, it ends here, and then you go around like that. And about the quarter of a block further back is, is where the street continued. Well, he lived right in that corner, that corner house there. And, uh, they took him to this, uh, Jesuit's church here at, at La Ola. What do they call it? The Little Flower or something like that? Right, the church at La Ola. Well, when, when, when the, when the, when the funeral left the house, got, by the time they got to La Ola, there still, there was people that still hadn't left the house. That's how many people they had at the funeral. And, it took full crossings of the ferry at Gretna, at Jackson Avenue. It took full crossings of the ferry to get, and a lot of the people didn't, they just went to the ferry, and that's all. You know, and didn't go across the river to the, to the cemetery. And it took full crossings of the ferry to get all the automobiles on there that, that went there.
Was that well known as a musician or as a musician?

As a, no, as a musician. He was not. He was. He, the, the, even, even the, even the, you know how the Cullfellas are. Yeah. You know, they don't talk much. But you can, you can ask any of the old, the real old timers about all of them. I've heard him call him.
